title: Sudama Finds His Hut a Palace
story:
Sudama walked the long road home from Dwaraka with empty hands, and his heart was strange with wonder. He had gone to see his old friend Krishna carrying a poor brahmin's gift, a single handful of flat rice, and Krishna had eaten it with delight, as if it were a feast prepared for a king. In the palace that night, any man in his place would have asked for help; his poverty had followed him all the way to Dwaraka, whispering of everything he lacked. But when he stood before Krishna, the words would not come. He could not ask for anything at all.

Now the villages of his own country were appearing one by one along the road, and he turned the marvel over in his mind. "Where am I," he asked himself, "poor and burdened with faults, and where is Krishna, the very home of fortune?" All his life he had measured the distance between them, and it had always seemed like the distance between mud and the moon. Yet Krishna had taken his handful of rice with love, and had given him back something he had not dared to imagine, and had done it without being asked, as though it were nothing.

Walking, he began to understand why. If he had asked for wealth and received it, would he have remembered? Wealth has a way of loosening a poor man's grip on everything else; it fills the hands and empties the heart. Krishna, who knew him through and through, had given him prosperity unasked, and in the giving had kept him still his friend. For the Lord, the wise say, does not hand his devotee the riches and glories that would pull the heart away from him; he gives what the heart can carry. And to Sudama he had given everything, because Sudama had asked for nothing but to remain his friend. "May this friendship, this companionship, this service to him," he prayed as he walked, "be mine in birth after birth."

He was still turning such thoughts when he came to the edge of his own village, and stopped, for he no longer knew it. Where his humble hut had stood there now rose a cluster of celestial mansions, ringed with gardens and clear lakes, their waters loud with the calling of birds. Well-dressed men and graceful women moved through the courtyards as though the place had always been theirs. Sudama stood in the road, a poor man in a worn cloth, and could not believe his eyes.

His wife heard that he had come, and hurried out to meet him, radiant as the goddess of fortune among her attendants. When she saw him her eyes filled with tears of love, and whatever hand had worked this change while he was away, she was still the same wife; she drew him, half laughing and half weeping, through the gates.

Inside, the wonder deepened. The beds were heaped soft as foam, spread with ivory and gold; jeweled lamps glowed in the rooms; the walls of crystal and emerald gave back the light of a hundred riches. Sudama, who had slept on a mud floor all his life, walked through his own house as though through a dream.

And there, among the golden couches, the truth of it settled on him at last. The Lord gives generously even to one who asks; how much more to a friend who asks for nothing? Krishna had accepted his single, meager handful of flat rice with joy, and had repaid it with a kingdom. It was not merely that Sudama had been given wealth, he realized. It was that Krishna had given it in such a way that the giving never came between them: unasked, unannounced, as natural as the return of an old friend.

That night, standing in the jewel-lit splendor of his own home, the poor brahmin who had gone to Dwaraka with empty hands found that he was rich beyond all measuring. Not in palaces, not in gold, but in this: that Krishna treasured even a handful of flat rice, and had turned an old friend's poverty into a palace without waiting to be asked.
reflection: Sudama's poverty is not ended by the palace but redefined by it. The story's quietest point is that Krishna gives generously even to those who ask, yet gives most safely to the friend who asks for nothing, and Sudama's prayer is not for wealth but that the friendship itself should continue birth after birth.
next_story_tease: The same grace was about to move on a grander stage, when Vasudeva himself would be initiated into a great sacrifice at Samanta-panchaka.
hero_scene: Sudama, in a worn cloth and carrying nothing, stands at the edge of his village gazing at the celestial mansions, gardens and lakes that have replaced his humble hut, while his radiant wife hurries toward him with tears of love in her eyes.
